title: Maximum Drawdown

statement.md: A risk report tracks the value of a strategy at the end of each day. The **drawdown** on day $j$ is how far the value has fallen from its highest earlier value, as a fraction of that peak. The **maximum drawdown** is the largest drawdown over the whole history.
A strategy that never falls below an earlier value has a maximum drawdown of $0$. Print the result as a fraction (not a percentage) with exactly 4 decimal places.

inputFormat: First line: $n$. Second line: $n$ equity values $v_1 \dots v_n$, each a positive number with at most two decimal digits.
outputFormat: One line: the maximum drawdown as a fraction with exactly 4 decimals, for example `0.2500`.
constraints: $0.01 \le v_i \le 10^6$, at most two decimal digits
No test value lies within $10^{-8}$ of a rounding tie at the fourth decimal
hints: Scan once and keep the running peak. At each day the drawdown is (peak - value) / peak.
The best peak for day j is the highest value seen up to and including day j, so one pass is enough.
editorial: [{"type": "p", "md": "Keep `peak = max(peak, v)` and `best = max(best, (peak - v) / peak)`. The peak that maximises the drawdown on day j is always the running maximum, so the pairwise $O(n^2)$ definition collapses to $O(n)$."}, {"type": "p", "md": "Drawdown is measured against the peak, not against the starting value. A curve that doubles and then halves has a drawdown of 0.5 from the peak even though it ends at its start."}]

solutions.python:
import sys


def main():
    tok = sys.stdin.read().split()
    n = int(tok[0])
    peak = 0.0
    worst = 0.0
    for s in tok[1:1 + n]:
        v = float(s)
        peak = max(peak, v)
        worst = max(worst, (peak - v) / peak)
    print(f"{worst:.4f}")


main()
